outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20, further strikes reported on subsequent days, including overnight and on the morning of Wednesday, Nov 25, and additional Wednesday afternoon strikes in several regions. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said the enemy continues to attack energy-infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, and that as a result, as of Thursday morning, there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv regions, with restoration work continuing wherever the security situation allowed. The same Thursday morning account said that because of damage to energy equipment, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all categories of consumers, and that current schedules should be checked on the official pages of the local distribution-system operator. That Thursday morning list of regions with de-energized consumers differed from Wednesday morning's five-region list, which had included Donetsk and had not named Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, or Chernihiv. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, and later Wednesday by Al Jazeera, had said Russia again attacked energy facilities overnight and on Wednesday morning, targeting power plants and electricity transmission and distribution substations, causing new power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25 report, quoted Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov as saying the situation was difficult in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk, where the attacks damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply. The Energy Ministry, as reported in those Wednesday morning accounts, and the IAEA, as reported by TASS citing an IAEA press-service statement, said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators. ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina, as reported by TASS on Nov 26 from Melitopol, said that as of the morning of Nov 26 the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when electricity would be restored. Ukrenergo, as reported Wednesday evening by Apostrophe at 9:23 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, and by 24 Kanal, had already said that on Thursday, Nov 26, stabilization measures would be in effect around the clock in a number of regions because of the consequences of strikes on energy-infrastructure facilities, with hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for household consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. Ukrenergo, as reported Thursday evening by RBC-Ukraine at 8:40 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said that on Friday, Nov 27, those planned restrictions would again be in effect throughout the day in some regions because of the consequences of attacks on the power system.

The same Thursday morning report said that because of damage to energy equipment, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all categories of consumers, and that current schedules should be checked on the official pages of the local distribution-system operator. TASS, in a Nov 26 report from Melitopol, quoted ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina as saying that as of the morning of Nov 26, the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when the line would be restored. The same TASS report said Yashina told the agency that backup diesel generators had started as expected, that staff were monitoring safety parameters, and that fuel reserves were available. The IAEA, as reported Wednesday by TASS citing an IAEA press-service statement, had said the plant completely lost its external power supply for the 28th time since the start of the conflict and switched to emergency diesel generators, and that the outage occurred at 5:28 a.m. Moscow time after the plant lost connection to its last operating external power line, Ferosplavna-1. Energoatom, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:56 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:56 a.m. CT), said that at 4:28 a.m. Wednesday a Russian attack on the right bank of the Dnipro River, 13 kilometers from the Ferosplavna substation, caused the 330 kV Ferrosplavna-1 transmission line to disconnect, and that the plant's essential systems were being powered by backup diesel generators. Earlier Wednesday, Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), had said that as of Wednesday morning there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions, that the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, and Al Jazeera, citing Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, likewise described new outages in those five regions after overnight and Wednesday-morning attacks, and said the situation remained most difficult in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk. Ukrenergo, as reported by Apostrophe at 9:23 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (1:23 p.m. CT), and by 24 Kanal, said that on Thursday, Nov 26, stabilization measures would be in effect throughout the day in a number of regions, with hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for household consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. Ukrenergo, as reported by RBC-Ukraine at 8:40 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (12:40 p.m. CT), said that on Friday, Nov 27, planned consumption restrictions would be in effect throughout the day in some regions of Ukraine: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for all other categories of consumers, because of the consequences of attacks on the power system, and that consumers should check current schedules on the official pages of their local distribution-system operator. UNN, in a Thursday report, likewise said Ukrenergo reported that Friday schedules would be in effect around the clock in a number of regions, with 0.5 to 3.5 groups planned to be disconnected, and wrote that one group means four hours without electricity, so outages may last from 2 to 14 hours. outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20, further damage reported over Nov 24-25, and a massive strike-drone attack on Odesa and its suburbs on the afternoon of Wednesday, Nov 25. Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region. Kiper, as reported later Wednesday by Censor.NET at 1:59 p.m. and by Kyiv Post, said Russian forces had launched a massive attack with strike drones against Odesa and its suburbs, targeting civilian and energy infrastructure. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported Wednesday morning by Odessa Life in an update at 7:54 a.m., said stabilization outages would be applied in Odesa and Odesa region on Wednesday, Nov 25, on Ukrenergo's command, and that schedules could be adjusted if Ukrenergo's commands changed. The same Odessa Life report, citing the company, also said urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district would leave that area without electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Wednesday, as previously announced. On Thursday, Nov 26, DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported by Odessa Life, said stabilization outages would apply in Odesa and Odesa region to all 12 of the company's schedule groups because of the consequences of attacks on the energy system. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, listed Odesa region among seven regions with de-energized consumers as of Thursday morning On Friday, Nov 27, DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported by Odessa Life at 10:52 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said stabilization outages would again apply in Odesa and Odesa region to all 12 of the company's schedule groups because of the consequences of attacks on the energy system.

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, including strikes on Nov 24 and overnight into Nov 25, a Wednesday, Nov 25, attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, and a later Wednesday attack that DTEK said damaged main power grids. DTEK, as reported Thursday morning by Dnepr.info, said emergency outages were in effect on Thursday, Nov 26, in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, where schedules were not in effect, and that stabilization outages continued in the rest of the region. DTEK, as reported Wednesday morning by UNN and by 5692.com.ua, said a massive Wednesday attack had stopped generation at one of the company's thermal power plants, had significantly damaged equipment, and was the company's third massive plant attack in November alone, and that because of the strikes, homes and part of critical infrastructure were left without electricity, with emergency outages by Ukrenergo order on Wednesday in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts. Ukrainska Pravda, in a report time-stamped 5:31 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, citing DTEK, and RBC-Ukraine, in a report time-stamped 4:30 p.m. Wednesday, also citing DTEK's official Telegram channel, said another Russian attack had damaged main power grids and again left parts of Dnipro and the same four districts without electricity. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, listed Dnipropetrovsk region among seven regions with de-energized consumers as of Thursday morning

outages.cause: Damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, according to JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo, including a further Wednesday attack that again cut power to some consumers after a partial restoration. The company's head, Andriy Stasevsky, in a Wednesday morning statement reported by Interfax-Ukraine, said a significant number of consumers in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity as a result of that damage, and that the emergency response plan for systemic power-grid failures had been activated. Later Wednesday, Zaporizhzhia regional military administration head Mykhailo Semikin, as reported by Ekonomichna Pravda at 4:24 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said the enemy had again damaged the region's energy infrastructure, and that people who had already had electricity restored after the mass outage were again without power. Stasevsky, in the same Ekonomichna Pravda report, said some consumers who had been re-energized after the mass outage were again without electricity, and that work to restore supply was continuing. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said the situation as of Wednesday morning remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where attacks had damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. An earlier Nov 22, 2026 report by The New Region had said the Monday meeting was planned to discuss resuming production, that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks, and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. No official customer count was given. No later official confirmation that Khor Mor production had already resumed was found as of 12:00 PM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (9:00 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Iraq time), three days after the Monday, Nov 23, meeting described in The New Region's Nov 23 report.

outages.place: Cauca, Nariño, Putumayo, Caquetá, and southern Huila
outages.cause: An attack on transmission infrastructure in southwestern Colombia on the afternoon of Nov 24, 2026, according to Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy, in a Nov 25 statement that said the attack had occurred the previous afternoon, and according to XM, the operator of the National Interconnected System. XM, in its official Thursday, Nov 26, update, also said that before this event the system had already been operating with a degraded network because of attacks a week earlier, leaving demand-serving capacity in the affected zone limited.
outages.affected: XM, the operator of Colombia's National Interconnected System, in an official update dated Nov 26, 2026, said that as a consequence of the Nov 24 transmission-network event in the country's southwest, affectations persisted in serving demand in Cauca, Nariño, Putumayo, Caquetá, and southern Huila, and that restoration was advancing according to operating conditions, with demand-serving capacity in the affected zone limited because the system had already been operating with a degraded network after attacks a week earlier. XM said that as of 8:00 a.m. Colombia time Thursday, Nov 26 (7:00 a.m. CT), recovery of service was around 80% of the forecast demand of the affected departments. XM said those percentages correspond to power served versus forecast demand at the cutoff time, not the share of customers or households with service, that the figures vary with restoration maneuvers, and that forecast demand is updated between communiqués, so a change in the percentage does not always mean less energy delivered. DataiFX, in a report published at 10:13 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, and updated at 11:24 a.m. Thursday, citing that Thursday XM update, gave these departmental figures as of the 8:00 a.m. cutoff: 200.7 MW served of 226.5 MW forecast in Cauca and Nariño (88.6%), 20.7 MW of 23.99 MW in Putumayo (86.3%), 21.7 MW of 43.22 MW in Caquetá (50.2%), and 31.1 MW of 50.43 MW in southern Huila (61.7%). XM also said further interruptions were possible because of reduced availability of national and regional transmission circuits, and that it was not possible to set an exact time for normalization. An earlier official XM update as of 6:00 p.m. Colombia time Wednesday, Nov 25 (5:00 p.m. CT), had said demand served, measured the same way, was 188 MW of 332 MW forecast in Cauca and Nariño (57%), 19.2 MW of 37 MW in Putumayo (52%), 28 MW of 69 MW in southern Huila (41%), and 24 MW of 60 MW in Caquetá (40%), according to those 6:00 p.m. figures as reported by BluRadio, citing XM. Earlier Wednesday, Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy, in a statement dated Nov 25, said that after an attack on electrical infrastructure the previous afternoon, the electrical system was serving about 68% of energy demand in the country's southwest, and it gave these morning figures: Putumayo 72%, Cauca and Nariño 71%, southern Huila 69%, and Caquetá 48%, which it called the most affected department. Diario del Sur, in a report dated 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:30 p.m. CT), said Electrocaquetá had partially restored service with 20 megawatts, and quoted distribution manager Jaime Zapata Franco as saying electricity was then available in Florencia, El Doncello, and part of Morelia, while the department's other municipalities remained without service. No official customer count was found as of 12:00 PM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (1:00 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Colombia time).

outages.cause: A collapse of a 275kV transmission tower in Ranau early Thursday morning, Nov 26, 2026, which Sabah Electricity said affected the west-to-east-coast transmission grid. The company's chief executive officer, Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star at 8:48 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time, said the tower's foundation along the banks of the Liwagu River was washed away following persistent heavy rains, resulting in the collapse of the tower, which is part of the grid that transmits 295 megawatts of electricity to the east coast. He said only the collapsed tower No. 313 needed to be replaced, that other nearby towers in Liwagu were not affected, that riverbank erosion had been detected during a routine aerial inspection in January and that rock and sand embankments had been constructed in March, and that existing generation capacity was insufficient to meet the area's overall demand. Borneo Post, in a report dated 9:25 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Sabah time (7:25 a.m. CT Thursday), quoted Yaakob as saying the 275kV Kolopis-Segaliud Line 1 and Line 2 tripped after the collapse of a transmission tower due to riverbank erosion along the Liwagu River. The Star, in a report dated 11:08 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (9:08 p.m. CT Thursday), quoting Sandakan Municipal Council president Datuk Walter Kenson, said the collapse was believed to have been caused by ground movement and continuous heavy rain and affected the 275kV Kolopis-Segaliud transmission line. Earlier Thursday accounts, including Daily Express and The Star, had identified the collapsed tower as T313 and said the incident, detected at 6:04 a.m. Thursday, disrupted two circuits and forced the closure of the main Ranau-Telupid or Ranau-Sandakan road. One passage in The Star's 8:48 p.m. report also referred to the tower as T133.
outages.affected: Sabah Electricity, in a Friday, Nov 27 statement reported by Malay Mail, first published at 1:38 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (11:38 p.m. CT Thursday, Nov 26) and last modified at 1:45 p.m. Friday (11:45 p.m. CT Thursday), said it is rationing power in eastern Sabah through coordinated feeder rotation schedules after transmission tower T313 collapsed in Ranau on Thursday, and that four districts were affected as of 10:00 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (8:00 p.m. CT Thursday): Sandakan, Tawau, Semporna, and Lahad Datu. A spokesperson said the utility is preparing a full rationing schedule, including the times involved, to be announced later. The same report said the collapse of tower T313, detected at 6:04 a.m. Thursday, severed two transmission circuits from Sabah's west coast to the east coast, disrupting electricity supply in eight districts, affecting 153,599 registered consumers. The Star, in a report dated 11:08 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (9:08 p.m. CT Thursday), quoted Sandakan Municipal Council president Datuk Walter Kenson, who is also Sandakan disaster management committee chairman, as saying that while efforts were under way to restore electricity supply through local power stations, their generation capacity was insufficient to meet the district's overall demand, and that power rationing in several areas in Sandakan was unavoidable. He said the district experienced a prolonged power outage from about 6:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. on Thursday, Nov 26, that Sabah Electricity was relying on power stations in Libaran, Batu Sapi, Labuk, Seguntor, and Mowtas to restore supply in Sandakan, and that the unstable electricity supply had also affected water-treatment-plant operations, forcing water rationing in several areas. Earlier, Sabah Electricity Chief Executive Officer Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star at 8:48 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time (6:48 a.m. CT Thursday), said the company had restored limited power generation in the state's east coast after the collapse, and that they expect to restore normal power supply to 153,000 consumers latest by Dec 3. He said they had restored limited power in the seven affected districts and that electricity supply capacity on the east coast would remain limited until the transmission lines were fully restored. He said Sabah Electricity would implement rotational power rationing in different areas starting immediately and would announce the schedules. The same Thursday evening report said repair teams and emergency transmission towers had been deployed to the site, and that eight generator sets had been mobilized, prioritizing critical facilities such as hospitals, schools, water treatment plants, and police stations. The districts named in that evening account were Sandakan, Lahad Datu, Tawau, Semporna, Kinabatangan, Kunak, and Beluran. Earlier Thursday accounts, including The Star at 7:15 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time (5:15 a.m. CT Thursday), had said eight districts — Sandakan, Tawau, Lahad Datu, Semporna, Kunak, Beluran, Telupid, and Kinabatangan — were affected by the outage that began at 6:04 a.m., that electricity had returned to parts of Tawau first, followed by parts of Sandakan, Semporna, and Telupid by afternoon, and that restoration to remaining areas was still under way.

He said they aim to restore the first transmission line on Dec 1 and both lines on Dec 2, but that because of conditions on the site they expect it to be fully restored by Dec 3. Borneo Post, in a report dated 9:25 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Sabah time (7:25 a.m. CT Thursday), quoted Yaakob as saying restoration work was expected to take six days, that Sabah Electricity aims to fully restore electricity supply to the east coast by Dec 2, and, during a media briefing, "in six days, we are certain to get the power back 100 per cent." The Star, in a report dated 11:08 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (9:08 p.m. CT Thursday), quoting Sandakan Municipal Council president Datuk Walter Kenson rather than Sabah Electricity, said repairs to the collapsed transmission tower in Ranau were expected to take between six and nine days. That report said Iribarren municipality, which includes Barquisimeto, was the most affected, with 16 outages in 16 communities totaling 85 hours and 57 minutes without power, and that Palavecino, Torres, and Simón Planas municipalities were also affected. That report did not give a nationwide customer count or a current official outage schedule. El Diario, last updated at 6:14 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Venezuela time (4:14 p.m. CT), said Corpoelec and the Ministry of Electric Energy were still working at the Coche substation to restore service progressively to more than 30 Caracas sectors, listed the same affected sectors, and said technical and operating crews were working without interruption to clear the fault as soon as possible; that report did not say the failure had already been fully cleared and did not give a customer count. outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. Democracy Now, in a Nov 24, 2026 headline, said Sudan's military reported intercepting drones launched by the Rapid Support Forces over Khartoum after attacks that struck the city's main airport and several buildings, including a U.N. facility, and that those attacks came as Sudan's power grid was on the brink of collapse following attacks on electricity stations; that headline did not state that the Nov 24 drone activity itself had struck power stations or give a customer count. No later official national customer count or official restoration timetable was found as of 12:00 PM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Sudan time).
